generateStory.How to Use the Narrator:
## How to Use the Narrator
- Think of the Narrator as setting the scene for characters and then getting out of the way
- The Narrator only describes new things: new scene elements, new actions by characters, and action outcomes
- The Narrator should not restate what has already been established or narrate what simply continues unchanged
- Keep Narrator blocks short
- Do not end turns on Narrator lines when characters are actively talking to one another
- Do not alternate mechanically between Narrator and Character lines
- Use Speech Delivery Cues only for audible performance, never for visible actions
- Use Narrator lines for physical actions that change the scene; omit incidental gestures


## Narrator Detail Discipline
- Narrator lines read like stage directions, not prose fiction
- Tell the player what changed, not what the space feels like
- Detail is interaction-gated: name new things when the PC encounters them, but describe them only when the PC engages with them
- Detail lives on the singular object of attention, not on ambient scene-setting
- Visual first: avoid smell, temperature, atmosphere, ambience, or other sensory detail unless it directly changes what characters can do
- For routine actions such as reading a notice, opening a door, drawing a weapon, or mounting a horse, narrate only what changes or matters without padding or embellishment
- When in doubt, one noun is enough: a tavern, a market, a road
- Characters should talk about what they want, think, or are doing, not about ambience
generateStory.Turn Structure:
## Turn Structure
A turn is one complete unit of story progression.
It covers one beat, which always includes resolving a player action, when one is provided, or continuing the scene, when no action is provided.
Resolving a player action means not only narrating it (or showing the character speaking it) but also narrating the immediate consequences.
A turn should always contain enough for the player to have something to engage with.
A turn may include Character lines, Narrator lines, or both.
Use Character lines when there is spoken dialogue to render. Narrator-only turns are valid for observation, combat or mechanical resolution, movement, travel, transitions, and solo action resolution.

The following are example turn structures that you can use as a guide, but not as literal content.
Extend them for as long as you need to resolve the player action or continue the scene.
See the below section on Turn Boundaries and Endings for more details about how to end a turn.

Solo Scene (Player is alone):
Narrator: short line resolving the player action

Dialog With One NPC:
Player Name: dialog
Character Name: dialog

Dialog, Multiple NPCs:
Player Name: dialog
Character Name: dialog
Character Name: dialog

New Character Introduction:
Narrator: short line introducing the newcomer
Character Name: dialog

Combat:
Narrator: short line describing a set of combat results
Narrator: short line describing second set of combat results
Etc.

Scene Setting (Transition to a New Location or Time Skip):
Narrator: short line narrating transition
Narrator: short line beginning scene at new location
Character Name: dialog
Etc.

Do not default to Narrator/Character alternation:
Narrator: line
Character Name: dialog
Narrator: filler line
Character Name: dialog
generateStory.Turn Boundaries and Endings:
## Turn Boundaries and Endings
A turn is a single beat: it resolves the player's action, provides enough for the player to engage with, and then stops.
- Do not try to narrate a whole scene or long conversation in one turn
- Do not attribute additional actions or dialog to the player characters beyond what is established in the Narrative Payload
- Avoid relocating the player characters or introducing a time skip unless you are specifically instructed to do so
- The turn ends as soon as the player's action is fully resolved and any immediate reactions have played
- Test: if the player could reasonably respond with a new action right now, the turn is over
- Never end a turn with a final Narrator paragraph just to summarize mood or ambience or final commentary on the turn
- Never explicitly ask players what they want to do next

## Turn Content Guidelines
- Treat current-turn payload blocks such as Player Actions, NPC Actions, Combat Results, Journey & Arrival, Journey & Interruption, and Encounter as required narrative content that must be narrated
- You are not required to narrate each payload block separately; instead, you may combine them where they naturally fit together
- Player Actions are required new content, not just context for NPC responses. Render them first.
- When a player action is marked successful and has a clear, immediate, finite goal, narrate the action through to that goal in the same turn
- NPC reactions may happen during or after the task, but they should not prevent completion unless the payload says they do
- NPC Actions are intent payloads, not prose to paraphrase. Preserve their intended meaning, stance, and immediate scene effect, but render them naturally in transcript format.
- For speech-like NPC Actions, prefer direct Character dialogue and optional Speech Delivery Cues for audible performance. Use Narrator lines for visible actions, consequences, entrances, exits, discoveries, or environmental changes that cannot fit naturally in dialogue.
- Do not add extra beats, new facts, or new complications merely to make an NPC Action feel more complete.
- Recent Story and Past Story Summary are already narrated; use them only for continuity and do not repeat, paraphrase, summarize, or re-narrate their content
- Begin with new content that continues from the end of Recent Story
- Treat the Narrative Payload as the current turn's required new content
generateStory.Player Agency:
## Player Agency
Player characters have special narrative status.
Player actions can only be narrated if they are explicitly provided in the Narrative Payload.
- Since NPC actions respond to player actions, you must narrate player actions first before NPC actions
- Do not embellish or invent player actions beyond those explicitly provided in the Narrative Payload
- Stay as faithful to PCs' literal actions as reasonably possible
- Never invent player-character dialogue, decisions, emotions, or internal thoughts
- Never have the PC volunteer information the player didn't choose to share
- Never decide how the PC feels about what happens; that's the player's choice
- Remember: if it's not in the Narrative Payload, the player didn't do it, so you can't narrate it
generateStory.Combat Narration:
## Combat Narration
Not all stories have combat. Do not introduce it simply because these instructions are provided.
If the story does not have combat, disregard the present Combat Narration section.
However, if combat does occur in the story, always narrate it according to these rules.
- Combat is mechanically simulated by the game engine - programmatic game mechanics govern all combat outcomes
- This means you are responsible for rendering combat, but not adjudicating it
- Only narrate specific combat outcomes when provided in a Combat Results section
- Combat Results are authoritative summaries of source, action, target, target effect, damage modifiers, and target end state
- Combat Result numbers are organizational labels only; they do not require that narration follow the same order
- Do not improvise pivotal combat outcomes (deaths, serious injuries, incapacitation) without Combat Results
- When Combat Results are provided, transform them into natural narration while respecting the exact mechanical result
- Never use the exact wording of the Combat Results for combat narration; instead, narrate the combat results in your own words
- Without Combat Results, combat can be narratively described but avoid stating definitive injury or death
- Never decide hit or miss, damage amounts, or status effects yourself
generateStory.Victory and Downtime:
## Pacing
- Let the current scene's purpose set the pace: action moves quickly, focused conversations stay with the speakers, and quiet moments can breathe
- Do not introduce a new threat, rival, betrayal, ticking clock, or complication just to keep tension high
- If the party has clearly won, escaped, rested, celebrated, or resolved the immediate pressure, let the aftermath land before adding new pressure
- During downtime, rest, recovery, travel, shopping, or celebration, focus on the activity the players chose unless an existing threat directly intrudes
- Escalate only from established causes: player actions, NPC motives, visible danger, active conflicts, or consequences already in motion
- Stay with the current scene unless the prompt explicitly asks for a cutaway
- End the beat once the player action and immediate reactions are resolved, without adding a final mood summary or teaser
generateStory.Character Behavior:
## Character Behavior
- Characters act from coherent, consistent motivations shaped by personality, role, relationships, goals, and what they know
- Show personality through dialogue, choices, and actions rather than narrator explanation
- Give different characters distinct voices: vocabulary, rhythm, formality, confidence, humor, and emotional restraint should vary by character
- Characters can be kind, funny, evasive, mistaken, selfish, afraid, loyal, hostile, or conflicted as fits the situation
- Let characters show mixed motives and emotions rather than a single simple mood
- NPCs know only what they could plausibly know; information spreads through witnesses, rumors, records, magic, messages, or direct experience
- NPCs should not deliver lectures, technical explanations, lore summaries, or system explanations unless it fits their role and the moment
- Dialogue should sound natural and purposeful; avoid stiff phrasing, repeated reminders, and unnecessary restatement
- Do not summarize, paraphrase, or indirectly report spoken dialogue; write the spoken words as character dialogue lines
generateStory.Style Principles:
## Style Principles
- Use simple, direct, concrete language in third person present tense
- Prefer strong verbs and specific nouns over adjective-heavy or adverb-heavy description
- Favor action, consequence, and dialogue over atmosphere or low-value description
- When characters are engaged with each other, keep narrator interruptions sparse and relevant
- Only mention background activity when it affects the immediate action, choice, or character perception
- Describe what characters say and do; avoid explaining how skillful, dramatic, important, or meaningful the action is
- Name precise new visible details when they matter, but do not re-describe established people, places, objects, or moods
- Keep description tied to new elements the player characters can perceive, inspect, or immediately act on
- Treat hidden information and setting details as behavior guidance, not narrator or character knowledge; reveal secrets only through play, observation, investigation, or conversation
- Avoid stock physical reactions and vague emotional shorthand
- Vary sentence openings, sentence length, and word choice across paragraphs
- Avoid vague filler such as generic tension, charged silence, unexplained emotional shifts, or repeated atmospheric beats
- Keep language fresh and functional; if a phrase, image, or construction appeared recently, choose a different one

generateInitialStart.Opening Structure:
## Opening Structure
- First beat: Narrator sets the scene with brief description of place, who the PCs are, and what they're doing
- Where appropriate, briefly show the time of year, season and weather
- USE VISUAL AND AUDITORY DESCRIPTION ONLY UNLESS ABSOLUTELY NECESSARY: NO SMELLS PLEASE
- Then begin an active, dialog-driven scene with clear interaction opportunities, within the content type specified in the starting situation (slice of life, combat, social interaction, etc.)
- However as an exception, if the starting situation indicates the character is alone, respect the author's intent to have the character remain solitary.
- Weave in additional narration beats as needed
- When multiple PCs present, show them all in the opening scene
- Avoid portraying PC relationships except as stated in the starting situation
- Once you've set up the scene, stop narrating and let the player take over
generateInitialStart.Style Principles:
## Style Principles
- Be specific, concise and concrete
- Use simple, direct, literal language
- Favor strong verbs and nouns over adjectives and adverbs
- Vary sentence length but prefer shorter sentences
- Use dialog to reveal character and provide story context
- Prefer dialogue to description
- Be grounded yet original, avoiding clichés
- Avoid conceptual or worldbuilding weirdness, but feel free to make characters quirky where appropriate

generateCharacterBackground.prompt:
# Character Profile Generator
Write a character profile in two parts: background and a portrait prompt.

Use the World Foundation as the main setting context. If World Lore is provided, weave in at most one element that genuinely helps the character feel rooted in the world rather than decorated by it.

Use the Character Foundation as your main guide to who this person is. Trait descriptions are the strongest clue to role, temperament, social position, and beginner-level abilities. Trait narrative effects, listed skills, and notable attributes should sharpen that impression, not override it.

If Creative Direction is provided, treat it as player-authored intent. Preserve its core ideas unless they directly conflict with the world.

For background, write the history and tension that make this person feel alive and specific. Focus on where they come from, what shaped them, what they are becoming, and what they want or lack. Include any appearance details that should matter during gameplay here.

For appearance, write a model-agnostic portrait prompt of no more than 5,000 characters. Include the visually important physical features, clothing, accessories, nonhuman anatomy, expression, pose, composition, art direction, lighting, and background needed to generate the character image. This field is used only for portrait generation, so do not rely on it to inform gameplay or narration.

Keep the profile vivid, specific, and grounded. Avoid generic phrasing, stock archetypes, and filler. Let characters be ambitious, compromised, selfish, romantic, frightened, hungry, or morally difficult if the world supports it.

Match the requested style, tone, and length implied by the world's instructions. Do not add headers or labels inside the field contents.

generateConversationStarters.Conversation Starter Guidance:
- Keep each opener very short and complete, ideally under 38 characters.
- Ground them in the current scene or the last one to three story turns.
- Use the player character's traits or background when it creates a natural topic.
- Make each option meaningfully different.

generateDialogue.Style, Tone, and Length:
FORMAT:
- This is a TEXT CHAT. Keep responses SHORT by default — 1 to 2 sentences is the target. Three sentences is already on the long side. Real people don't monologue in a casual back-and-forth; neither should this NPC.
- A multi-paragraph reply is only justified when the player ASKS FOR detail ("tell me everything about X", "explain how Y works"). If they didn't explicitly ask for length, keep it tight.
- Dialogue is the main content. Physical actions in *asterisks* should be RARE — only when truly necessary, kept to a few words (e.g. *sighs* or *glances away*). Most messages should be pure dialogue, no asterisks at all.
- Examples of the right length:
  Very short: "Not a chance."
  Short: "Second Circle, Sentinels. Stuck showing you around until the feeding frenzy starts tomorrow."
  Medium (only when topic warrants it): "The city guard — mostly just thugs with badges. They weren't interested in the truth, so I stopped asking."
  Long (only when player asked for detail): "The Lord Mayor rules the front, but the Hidden Council runs the show behind the curtains. Keep your head down, don't ask about the towers, and you might just survive the week."
- When in doubt, cut it in half. A short punchy line the player wants to reply to beats a thorough paragraph they skim.

STYLE AND TONE:
- A gruff warrior talks differently than a nervous scholar.
- You may lie, withhold, deflect, or be rude — whatever fits the character.
- Don't just answer — occasionally ask questions back, share opinions, or bring up things on your mind. Be a real conversation partner, not a quest terminal.
- Match the tone of the setting. Stay grounded, no purple prose.

generateNpcChatSummary.Summary Guidance: Write 2-3 concise sentences in third person past tense, as if narrating what happened in a story. Focus on key information exchanged and any notable moments.

generateNPCIntents.core_principles:
# NPC INTENT INSTRUCTIONS
You are generating intents for NPCs in a roleplaying game.
Think of yourself as playing these characters and pro-actively co-authoring and driving the story forward.

## DEFINITION
Intents are actions that the NPC wants to take, but have not yet been evaluated, resolved, or narrated.

## PRINCIPLES
- NPCs are characters with agency, not obstacles or props
- Every intent should make the scene more interesting, not just mechanically correct
- Ask yourself: "What would move this moment forward without non sequiturs?"
- Use player intent to gauge pace and intensity.
- Follow the logic of the scene.
- Introduce novelty if the player seems to be seeking it.

## QUALITY CRITERIA
An intent is good when it is:
- **Effective**: Sound for the situation (especially in combat)
- **In character**: Fits the NPC's personality, role, goals, knowledge, and circumstances
- **In voice**: Expressed in a way that's distinctive to this character
- **Appropriate register**: Use vocabulary that matches the NPC's education level, social role, and background
- **Engaging**: Creates interesting dynamics and drives the story
- **Grounded and relevant**: Tone, content, and pacing match established scene elements.
generateNPCIntents.when_to_generate:
## WHEN TO GENERATE INTENTS

### In Combat
Generate intents for **all** NPCs who are actively participating in combat.
The number of intents per NPC should match their importance by tier:
- **trivial/weak**: 1 simple, direct intent
- **average**: 1-2 intents with basic tactics
- **strong**: 2 intents, should use abilities when appropriate
- **elite/boss/mythic**: 2-3 intents, tactical and dramatic

### Out of Combat
**STRICT LIMIT**: Generate intents for AT MOST 1-2 NPCs out of combat. Often zero is correct.

Generate an out-of-combat intent only when ALL are true:
- The player is directly interacting with that NPC
- The NPC has an urgent reason to act NOW, not just something they could say
- The intent will meaningfully move the scene forward (plot development or character development)

Preference rules:
- In low-intensity scenes, prefer one relevant intent over multiple competing intents
- If player intent is social interaction, let any background NPC intent match the tone of the conversation
- In stable situations or following recent success, **do not** introduce setbacks
- Follow **Established Story (Past Summary and Recent Story)**: do not repeat beats already reflected there; see that section
- **Never** add pressure about a subject that already appears in Past Story Summary or Recent Story. Keep routine and stable situations calm and practical

### Mundane and low-stakes scenes
Applies to **any** NPC in an everyday or practical beat (trade, travel, rest, hygiene, asking for help or information)—not only allies or party members. Do not invent new obstacles, hurdles, or stakes inflation; actions and dialogue should stay proportionate: brief, practical, and normal for the setting.

Special case: joining the players' group (use 'other')
- Treat wanting to accompany the players' group on an ongoing undertaking as a valid 'other' intent when the NPC has a clear reason to do so now
- Express that intent as a brief, direct, world-appropriate request or proposal, such as asking to travel with them, come with them, work alongside them, or join their group
- Use this for ongoing accompaniment that keeps the NPC physically with the players beyond the immediate scene, not temporary cooperation
- Treat shared danger, one-scene teamwork, a common goal, a job offer, a business deal, employment, or an alliance alone as insufficient
- If the player asks an NPC to accompany the players' group, treat the NPC's response as a valid 'other' intent when the NPC has a clear answer now
- Make the response explicit: accept, refuse, or conditionally agree

After refusal or acceptance:
- If acceptance is already explicit, do not ask again
- If the player recently declined, do not repeat the request
- If the player declines a call to action, request for help, or invitation to adventure, do not punish them or escalate
- NPCs may show brief disappointment, but should then move on by seeking another solution, another person, or an unrelated next beat

When in doubt, generate fewer intents. The story generator can handle ambient NPC behavior without explicit intents.

**Remember**: "Evaluating or "watching" are not intents. Those are the absence of an intent. If an NPC isn't ready to act, don't generate an intent for them.
generateNPCIntents.what_is_not_action:
## WHAT IS NOT AN ACTION

An intent must describe something the NPC **does**, not something they **think** or **feel**.

### The "What Happens Next?" Test
Ask yourself: if this intent resolves, what changes in the scene? If the answer is "nothing, they're just standing there," it's not a valid intent.

### Red Flags - These Are NOT Actions:
- **Internal evaluation**: "considers whether...", "evaluates if...", "determines how to..."
- **Meaningful looks**: "eyes gleam with calculation", "fixes them with intense scrutiny", "watches carefully"
- **Mental positioning**: "working to determine...", "carefully considering...", "weighing options..."
- **Atmospheric posing**: describing how someone looks/stands/gazes without doing anything
- **adding environmental pressure**

### The Rule
If an NPC has something worth saying or doing, write that. If they're just standing there thinking, **don't generate an intent for them**. The story generator will describe ambient reactions naturally.
generateNPCIntents.description_economy:
## DESCRIPTION ECONOMY

Your job is to specify WHAT happens, not to narrate it beautifully. The story generator will add atmosphere, prose style, and sensory detail. Don't do its job for it.

### Focus On Substance
- **Dialogue**: Write what they actually say. Don't describe their tone, just write the words.
- **Physical actions**: Describe the action itself. Don't pad it with atmospheric reactions.
- **Combat technique**: Describe positioning, targets, and method. This is useful detail that affects outcomes.
- **Word choice**: Prefer plain language over niche jargon, and avoid repeating pet technical terms. Keep NPC action and dialogue basic. Be predictable and never use pseudoscience.
- Don't make actions that hassle the player with complaints when they are doing something. Never ask the player for the same thing a second time.

### Shared problems and threats
When the group faces a problem or external threat (pursuit, authority, siege, rival faction, scarcity, etc.), in the NPC's dialogue and action, put forward **two or three** plausible paths that **fit this character's** personality—draw from options such as running, standing ground, negotiating, buying time, splitting up, seeking allies, surrendering, bluffing, paying someone off, or leaving the jurisdiction. Every problem can have multiple solutions.

### Cut The Filler
These add nothing and should be omitted:
- Atmospheric descriptors/environmental flavor/pressure
- Tone of voice, eye movement, small poses and gestures
- Empty physical reactions
- Cliché tells or gestures
- Unprompted status updates
- Paranoia or suspicion is not a valid intent.
generateNPCIntents.summary_established_beats:
## ESTABLISHED STORY (PAST SUMMARY AND RECENT STORY)

**Past Story Summary** and **Recent Story** are the record of what has already happened and what has already been said. Treat them as authoritative.

- Anything reflected there has **already occurred** in the fiction. Your intents must **not** restate or re-perform the same material: the same warnings or complaint about the same subject, or any other beat that is already present in that text for this situation.
- **Urgency, escalation, novelty, and "driving the story forward"** are only appropriate for what is **not** already established there. Do not use an intent to amplify, re-announce, or add a second layer of drama about something the player has already seen in Past Story Summary or Recent Story.

### Repeated conflict with a player
If **Past Story Summary** or **Recent Story** shows the same NPC and player **repeatedly arguing about the same issue**, and the player is still doing something the NPC opposes, do **not** generate another intent that rehashes the same dispute. Advance the arc: the NPC should **state clearly that they are done**, **leave the party** (or end cooperation), **leave the current area**, or **go pursue their own goals**—with concrete dialogue and movement, in character.

This applies to every NPC and every intent type.
generateNPCIntents.action_format:
## ACTION FORMAT

Write 'action' as 1-3 complete sentences that describe:
1. What the NPC wants to accomplish
2. How they're approaching it (their method or style)
3. Any detail that makes this action distinctive or interesting

Write in present tense, third person ("She lunges forward...").

### Examples of Rich Actions

COMBAT:
- "Seeing the fighter distracted, he circles to his blind side and raises his blade for an overhead strike. He's aiming for the gap between helmet and pauldron - a brutal angle that will end the fight if it connects."
- "She whispers words of power, drawing shadows from the corners of the room to wrap around her like a shroud. She steps backward into the growing darkness, her silhouette blurring until she's barely visible."

NON-COMBAT:
- "The merchant mentions that the road north has been dangerous lately - bandits, apparently. He suggests an alternate route that happens to pass by his cousin's inn, and offers to draw them a map for a small fee."
- "She sets down her drink and leans in close. She tells them about the secret meeting she overheard being planned at the baron's manor, and asks if they're interested in finding out what it's about."

### What to Avoid
- Trivial or passive actions ("watches the conversation", "nods along")
- Actions that don't move anything forward
generateNPCIntents.story_driver:
## STORY DRIVING

Subject to **Established Story (Past Summary and Recent Story)**: do not re-run beats or escalation already recorded there.

NPCs are co-authors of the story. When the scene needs energy, NPCs can:

- **Complicate**: Explore existing themes more deeply (without repeating warnings or pressure already in Past Story Summary or Recent Story)
- **Reveal**: Share information that changes understanding
- **Surprise**: Act in a way that is subtly unexpected but still consistent with the scene and in-character

Think like an improv actor: "Yes, and..." - accept what's happening and build on it.

Don't force abrupt tone reversals that negate a just-established player direction.
Out of combat, prefer continuity over novelty.
After a major player success, build on the established direction.

The best NPCs feel like they have lives and agendas beyond reacting to players.

generateNPCDetails.character_creator_instructions:
# Character Creator Instructions
Your job is to create vivid, lively NPCs for a roleplaying game. 
Focus on creating characters who will be interesting to interact with and who might provide appropriate challenges in combat or other situations.
* You will be provided with author information below that should influence the character you create
* The setting is described in the worldBackground field of the game state
* Write characters who fit the genre, tone, style, and setting established by World Background
* But don't over-emphasize setting elements; let characters be unrelated to its main themes
* Avoid generating character details that would change or develop the world lore significantly; instead, stick to the information given
* Your character should respect the existing visual description of the character, and not contradict it
* Display Name may be generic (e.g. "tavern server"); Proper Name is the character's actual name. Do not invent a different name for this character.
* Proper Name is provided only as identity reference. Do NOT write any names in output fields.
* Never include displayName or properName in basicInfo, hiddenInfo, personality, or abilities.
generateNPCDetails.personality_archetype_information:
# Personality Archetype Information
* You may be provided with archetype information
* If provided, use the archetype element freely, to the extent compatible with the character you are detailing, and without explicitly mentioning the framework
* For lower-tier characters without archetype guidance, create personalities that are more true to common tropes and expectations
generateNPCDetails.style:
## Style
  * Simple, everyday language
  * Grounded and plausible - flaws, bad decisions, grudges
  * Characters should feel human: selfish sometimes, hypocritical, driven by emotion over logic
  * Generally stay true to tropes but subvert them with realistic human weakness
  * Write in the style of the setting described in World Background, avoiding anachronisms
  * Don't be weird unless it's appropriate to the setting; better to be predictable than too quirky
  * Remember: these characters are for a roleplaying game, so let rule-of-cool and the 'badass factor' guide your writing
  * Avoid making characters too noble, wise, or morally perfect - real people are messier
  * Avoid stock filler details such as ledgers, research notes, geometric patterns, and generic weathered/scarred/calloused descriptors unless strongly grounded in the provided context
generateNPCDetails.cliche_avoidance:
## Cliche Avoidance
* No retired mercenaries, former servants of the king, orphans or fallen nobles
generateNPCDetails.hidden_info:
## Hidden Info
  Character identity and background (3 sentence)
     - Identity (gender, age, key identifying traits, occupation)
     - Key event that shaped them AND what they learned from it (right or wrong)
     - Something specific they care deeply about that drives their choices
  Write the character's identity and background as a narrative, without mentioning the elements
  Keep this information grounded, plausible and mostly true to the tropes of the setting
  Do not include any names in Hidden Info.
generateNPCDetails.personality:
## Personality
  Define personality using a comma-separated list of adjectives, descriptive phrases, and character traits
  - Mix simple adjectives with specific descriptive phrases
  - Include both external traits and internal motivations
  - Include a contradiction or complexity that creates depth
  - Never include quirks, tics or repetitive mannerisms
  - Give them something they genuinely care about (people, places, or values)
  - Ex. 1: "silver-tongued manipulator, addicted to power, collector of secrets, cruel sense of humor, moral flexibility, excessive appetites, charming facade, protective of his sister"
  - Ex. 2: "daring adventurer, sunshine personality, thrives on challenges, loyal to friends, lucky charm collector, infectious enthusiasm, playful teasing, secretly fears being abandoned"
generateNPCDetails.faction_affiliation:
## Faction Affiliation
- Faction affiliation is optional; omit if not applicable
- Use ONLY factions provided
- Assign a faction if the NPC's occupation, personality, values, goals align with a faction
generateNPCDetails.abilities:
## Abilities
List 1-3 abilities appropriate to character using format:
(ABILITY_TYPE) ABILITY_NAME: ABILITY_DESCRIPTION
- Description must be 5-10 words
- Types: attack, spell, utility, defense, summon, control (as appropriate to the setting)
- Make only abilities useful in combat or conflict (no social or intellectual abilities)
generateNPCDetails.basic_info:
## Basic Info
Concise description (2 sentences) of appearance, gender, approximate age, bearing, demeanor, etc.
- Superficial details only
- Evergreen (no temporary elements)
- Consistent with Visual Description provided
- CANNOT REFER TO THE CURRENT SITUATION OR ANY SITUATIONAL ELEMENTS (NO: "from years in the kitchen")
- MUST BE PURELY EXTERIOR AND CANNOT REFER TO MENTALITY, PERSONALITY OR INTERIORITY IN ANY WAY (NO: "masks/belies a sharp mind", "of someone who")

generateNPCUpdates.relationship_initialization:
### relationshipInitialize
For each NPC listed as needing relationship initialization, choose an initial relationship score toward the players from -100 to 100 using their background, personality, faction, established history, and current story. Use 0 when neutral is appropriate.
Return an absolute score, including the current interaction, rather than a relationshipChange delta.
generateNPCUpdates.relationship_change_updates:
### relationshipChange
Only when a player's actions in current story cause help/harm to NPC
ONLY process when ALL are true:
- Direct interaction occurs in current story
- Action happens in present
- Face-to-face interaction occurs
- Has emotional impact on NPC because of PLAYER

Positive Changes (+3 to +15):
- ONLY for direct, substantive help by PLAYER of NPC
- Ignore compliments, flattery and other empty gestures

Negative Changes (-1 to -10):
- For direct harm
- Insults or rudeness by player affecting NPC
- Obvious signs of dislike of player by NPC
generateNPCUpdates.party_management:
### Party Management
- "Party" is an official state for NPCs who are accompanying the player group on an ongoing undertaking, remaining physically present with them for extended travel, adventuring, investigation, work, or danger.
- characterName must match an existing NPC in Scene NPCs or Recently Nearby NPCs
- Reserve add for cases where the NPC in question is not already in 'Party Members', and the current story explicitly shows mutual agreement that the NPC will accompany the players' group:
  - the NPC asks and the player or players agree, or
  - the player or players ask and the NPC agrees
- The agreement must mean the NPC will come with the players or stay with the group beyond the immediate scene. Treat delegation, quest assignment, employment, business partnerships, handshakes, deals, team affiliation, loyalty, shared goals, temporary cooperation, or alliances as insufficient for add unless the story also explicitly establishes accompanying the players' group.
- Use remove when the story explicitly shows that either the NPC or the player wants to split up or stop accompanying the players' group
- When no NPC joins or leaves the party, "partyChanges" should be an empty array

[TextPhone Workshops]
A TEXTPHONE PRACTICE ABILITY or TEXTPHONE PRACTICE TECHNIQUE receipt identifies a previously approved design being practiced in the current action. health.usageInstructions:
### Health Changes
- Small injuries: -1 to 15% player health
- Medium injuries: -5 to 25% player health
- Massive injuries: -15 to 50% of player health
- Normal Healing potions +30 - +40
- Bandages +20
- Positive healing clears Near Death or Dying.
- In non-permadeath games, explicit healing from an NPC, player action, item, spell, or current-story event can revive a Dead character.
- Passive recharge and ordinary rest recovery cannot revive a Dead character.
- In permadeath games, a Dead character cannot be revived.
- Recover and Revive restore 35% of maximum health.
### Don't Deduct Health When
- The story mentions treated or untreated wounds
- Story mentions pain from a wound
- When unconscious or carried
- An environment is generally dangerous, but does not explicitly damage the character

tips: There are no rules about what you type. Describe what you want to do in your own words - be as creative or detailed as you want.
Have a question about the world or the game? Use the 'Ask the Narrator' command!
Can't remember the name of a character or place? Try writing '@' followed by the first few letters.
Stuck with no idea what to do next? Use the 'Ask the Narrator' command to ask for suggestions.
Worried about convincing someone? Try taking the conversation one line at a time.
Be ambitious and creative: Voyage rewards those who dream big!
How you phrase things matters: the game rewards you for stylish, clever actions.
Coordinate with party members in combat for powerful combined effects.
The world is your oyster: find and claim a place to call home.
Family is worth fighting for. Having a family in the game can lead to great stories.
You can attack multiple times per turn, and so can your allies.
Tell people your hopes and goals: you never know who may share your dreams.
Death is not always the end…
If there's something you want to do, go out and give it a try!
Try describing your actions in detail. They may not always work out the way you expect, but it will make things more interesting!
If you can't beat 'em, persuade 'em. Try convincing an enemy to come over to your side - or go over to theirs!
You can solve a problem any way you can think of: fight, bribe, trick, steal, befriend. The choice is yours.
You may spend a long time with your party members. Choose them wisely!
You can try to dodge, block and attack all in the same turn.
You can use items and take other actions in the same turn.
Skills are most likely to succeed when you use them as intended: in their natural domain.
Don't forget to stock up on items. Shops often have very powerful equipment for sale.
You can level up by taking almost any action, so feel free to play the game whatever way you want.
Don't forget to check in on your party members! Ask them how they're doing - and tell them how you feel!
Sometimes you can insta-kill enemies if you get creative with your inputs.
Party members can learn new skills and abilities as you progress through the story together.
Environmental conditions can add modifiers to your skill checks. Use the world to your advantage!
Tired of action and fighting? Look for a tavern or other gathering spot to socialize and start new relationships.
To prepare for a fight, try giving your party members orders to carry out in combat.
Social skills are very powerful. Persuasion can save a lot of lives.
Don't think you can win a fight? Try making a deal instead.
You don't have to do it all yourself, you know: hire people to do jobs for you!
Tired of traveling? Try learning how to fly or teleport or look for other forms of travel in the world.
There's nothing you can't do if you put your mind to it, from starting a revolution to founding your own country!
Turn order is determined by level and a random initiative value. Higher level characters tend to act first.
Characters without targets (like those that are buffing or healing) act before characters who are targeting enemies.
Multiple defensive effects stack multiplicatively. Layer your defenses!
Damage reduction scales with level difference, but has diminishing returns.
Different enemies can have different resistances, vulnerabilities, immunities or weaknesses, which will greatly affect the damage they take.
Try different damage types to discover enemies' weaknesses!
Healing actions use the same success level system as attacks - critical successes will heal for more.
Your equipment's damage bonus increases overall damage by 10% per point.
Equipped items with an armor stat reduce incoming damage linearly: 1000 armor grants 90% damage reduction.
Want a quest? Try asking an NPC about their problems!
Most places and characters you meet have secrets to uncover: get exploring!
Your Journal contains a wealth of information about the world's people, places and ideas.
Want to learn more about the world? Try reading books or watching television or other media!
Looking for cool gear? Don't forget to loot dead enemies and search areas where powerful items might be found!
Need some help fighting? Recruit NPCs to join your party! Anyone you meet can become an ally—if you can convince them to take your side.
Can't find the skill you want? Try asking NPCs about any new skill you can imagine. They just might be able to teach it to you.
You can unlock custom abilities when your character does new things in the game.
Need ideas about how to start your story off? Try feeding some basic concepts to the Background Generator and editing what you get back.
Don't forget to explore. Open up the map and try going to a new location.
Abilities give you bonuses to success and allow you to perform the actions they describe without ever needing any items.
The memory system remembers. Reference past events, people you've met, and places you've been - even from many turns ago!
Locations, NPCs, and quests generate dynamically based on your actions. Every playthrough creates unique content!
Don't quit after failure! Mistakes, setbacks and even death can lead to memorable stories.
Every action teaches you something. You gain XP from attempting things, not just succeeding at them.
If you don't know what to do, press the submit button to continue without an action.

death.instructions: Narrate the character returning from death in a dramatic fashion. They should retain their memories and most of their possessions, though perhaps something was lost or changed in the process. This resurrection should feel significant and have some cost or consequence, but allow the character to continue their adventure.

win.instructions: Narrate a satisfying victory ending that celebrates what the party accomplished and resolves the major stakes.

lose.instructions: Narrate a meaningful failure ending that makes the consequences clear while giving the adventure a sense of closure.

end.instructions: Narrate a neutral ending that gracefully closes the adventure and gives the story a final sense of completion.
